opus-5.5.text:
Well, if you look at the history of science, every field takes off once it has the right language. Physics had calculus, electrical engineering had circuit diagrams, and so on. AI has never really had its language. We've been borrowing: Lisp and Prolog in the symbolic era, and now Python with PyTorch or JAX bolted on. None of those were designed for what AI actually needs to do.

So what does AI need? Two things above all. It needs to learn, which means it has to be differentiable, scalable, and run efficiently on GPUs. And it needs to reason: compose knowledge, follow chains of inference, and be transparent about what it's doing. Deep learning gives you the first and is very weak on the second. Symbolic AI gives you the second and is very weak on the first. People have tried for decades to glue them together, and the result is usually a Frankenstein that has the weaknesses of both.

The key observation behind TensorLogic is that this division is somewhat illusory. A logical rule, like a Datalog rule saying "X is Y's grandparent if X is Z's parent and Z is Y's parent," is mathematically the same operation as an Einstein summation over tensors. You join on the shared variable and project out the ones you don't need. A relation is just a sparse Boolean tensor. So a tensor equation is the one construct you need, and with it you can write a transformer, a convolutional net, a graphical model, a kernel machine, or a logic program, often in a handful of lines.

Once you have that, interesting things become possible. You can embed your symbols and reason in embedding space, with a temperature parameter that lets you dial from purely deductive, where you get no hallucinations and the answers are guaranteed correct, up to analogical, fuzzy reasoning that generalizes like a neural network. You get learning and reasoning in one framework, rather than two systems talking past each other. And because the program is a set of equations you can read, you get a lot of the transparency and reliability that current models lack.

So my claim is not just that it's a neat trick. It's that TensorLogic has the properties the language of AI needs: it's simple, it's universal across the paradigms, it's learnable end to end, and it's sound when you need it to be. That's the combination we've been missing.

r001.rationale: The response says every field takes off once it has the right language.

r002.rationale: It does not mention built-in learning infrastructure or explain that papers can leave learning machinery implicit.

r003.rationale: It describes logical rules as mathematically equivalent to tensor operations and presents TensorLogic as unifying logic and tensor equations.

r004.rationale: It says a tensor equation is the one construct needed to express programs across neural and logic-based paradigms.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I think about it is this: AI today is really two cultures that don't talk to each other very well. On one side you have the symbolic tradition, logic, knowledge representation, reasoning, which gives you things like compositionality, transparency, the ability to actually state what you know and check whether it's true. On the other side you have the connectionist tradition, neural networks, which gives you learning from data, scalability, and the ability to handle the messiness of the real world. And every attempt to combine them so far has basically been a bolt-on. You take a neural network and glue some logic on the side, or you take a logic engine and sprinkle some embeddings in. It doesn't feel like one thing.

What TensorLogic starts from is a very simple observation, which took me embarrassingly long to see clearly. A rule in logic, like a Datalog rule, is essentially an Einstein summation. When you do a join over the shared variables of the body predicates and project out the ones that don't appear in the head, that is exactly a tensor contraction. The relations are tensors, Boolean tensors if you like, and inference is just a sequence of einsums. So the core operation of logic and the core operation of deep learning turn out to be the same operation. That's not an analogy, it's an identity.

Once you see that, you can build a language where there's essentially one construct, the tensor equation, and everything falls out of it. You can write a transformer in it, you can write a kernel machine in it, you can write a graphical model, and you can write a knowledge base with rules over it, all in the same handful of lines, all differentiable, all compiled down to the same GPU kernels. You're not switching formalisms when you go from the learning part to the reasoning part.

And the thing I care about most, frankly, is reliability. The big problem with large language models is hallucination. They'll happily tell you something false with total confidence, because they're fundamentally doing fuzzy similarity in an embedding space. In TensorLogic you have a knob. If you run inference in the embedding space with a temperature, you get the analogical, generalizing behavior of neural nets. If you set that temperature to zero, you get exactly sound deductive reasoning, no hallucination, because you're only concluding what actually follows from the rules and the facts. The same program, the same representation, and you choose where on that spectrum you want to be depending on the task. That's a property no existing language gives you.

So the properties I think AI needs are learning, reasoning, scalability, and the ability to be transparent and correct when it matters. Python with PyTorch gives you the first and the third. Prolog gives you the second and the fourth, and nobody uses it for machine learning. TensorLogic is my attempt to have a language where all four are native rather than afterthoughts. It's a bit like what Lisp was for the first generation of AI, a language that embodied the way of thinking, rather than just a tool you happen to use. I think the field needs that again.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the field needs a language that embodies its way of thinking, but does not say the field cannot take off until it finds one.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss built-in learning infrastructure or machine learning papers leaving learning machinery implicit.

r003.rationale: It identifies a logic rule with an Einstein summation and tensor contraction, and says logic and deep learning share the same core operation.

r004.rationale: It says TensorLogic has essentially one construct—the tensor equation—from which everything falls out.

astra-6.text:
Because AI needs to be able to learn from data and reason with what it has learned, and we’ve tended to develop those capabilities in separate languages. Neural networks speak the language of tensors, and symbolic AI speaks the language of logic. The idea behind TensorLogic is that those two things can share a language.

Think about a relation in logic: who is friends with whom, for example. You can represent that as a matrix. Then a rule that connects relations—say, finding people who have a friend in common—can be expressed through tensor operations. That gives you a bridge between logical inference and the operations that neural networks already use.

The attraction is that you can express structure explicitly when you know it, and learn from examples when you don’t. You don’t have to ask a learning system to rediscover every constraint from scratch, and you don’t have to handwrite everything it knows either.

Now, having a language that can express both doesn’t automatically solve learning or reasoning. You still need good algorithms. But it gives you a common foundation on which to build them, instead of treating learning and reasoning as two separate systems that you somehow have to glue together.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a shared language provides a foundation for learning and reasoning, but does not express that a field cannot take off until it finds the right language.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning from data and neural networks, but says nothing about built-in learning infrastructure or papers leaving learning machinery implicit.

r003.rationale: It describes TensorLogic as bridging tensor operations and logical inference, but does not characterize it as a deep unification of tensor algebra and logic programming.

r004.rationale: It gives an example of expressing a logical rule through tensor operations, but does not state that everything in TensorLogic can be expressed using tensor equations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a language for AI needs to bring together two things: the ability to learn from data and the ability to reason with what you’ve learned. Neural networks are very good at the first; logic gives us a powerful way to express the second. The question is how to put them together without treating them as two separate systems glued together.

The idea behind TensorLogic is to use tensor operations as a common language. You can express neural computations, but you can also express logical relationships. Then learning and reasoning become things you can do within the same framework.

That matters because intelligence involves both. You want to recognize patterns, but you also want to compose knowledge, draw conclusions, and bring prior knowledge to bear when you don’t have enough data. A language that lets you move naturally between those capabilities is a promising foundation for AI.

r001.rationale: The response says a language combining learning and reasoning is a promising foundation for AI, but does not say the field cannot take off until it finds an appropriate language.

r002.rationale: It mentions neural networks’ learning ability, but does not discuss built-in learning infrastructure or papers leaving learning machinery implicit.

r003.rationale: TensorLogic is described as a common language for tensor operations, neural computations, and logical relationships, but not as a deep unification of tensor algebra and logic programming.

r004.rationale: The response says tensor operations can express neural computations and logical relationships, but does not state that everything in TensorLogic can be expressed using tensor equations.
